source: Electricity flowing through a coil of wire makes a magnet that can be turned on and off. Electromagnets lift scrap metal and turn the motors in fans and toys.
Thinking an electromagnet stays a magnet after the current stops. Switch the current off and it lets go.
In 1820 a Danish professor, Hans Christian Ørsted, noticed during a lecture that a compass needle jumped when he switched on a current in a nearby wire. Electricity can make magnetism!
A coil of wire with electricity flowing through it is a magnet, an electromagnet. Wrap it around an iron nail and it gets stronger. Switch off the current and it stops being a magnet.
An electromagnet: a battery, a switch and a coil of wire around an iron nail. Close the switch and the nail picks up paper clips.

Electromagnets are in doorbells, speakers, cranes that lift scrap cars, and electric motors. A motor uses electromagnets pushing and pulling on magnets to make something spin: a fan, a mixer, a toy car.
A scrapyard crane lifts a car, moves it and drops it in a pile. Why use an electromagnet instead of a regular magnet?
So it can drop the car when the current is switched off.
A regular magnet cannot be switched off.
An electromagnet lets go the moment the current stops.
Thinking an electromagnet stays magnetic forever. It is a magnet only while the current flows (a steel nail may keep a little magnetism).
Going further. Michael Faraday turned this idea into the first motor and generator: Faraday: Experimental Researches in Electricity. Later: Electromagnets in Physical Science.
